Someone asked:
"Which is more difficult, offering advice or accepting it?"
He replied:
"Offering advice is difficult,
because accepting it is difficult.
If accepting advice were not difficult,
then offering advice would be easy."
Someone asked:
"Which is more difficult, knowing others or knowing oneself?"
He replied:
"Knowing oneself is to seek within and what is near;
knowing others is to seek without and what is distant.
Knowing others is difficult.
If you exhaustively examine its possibilities,
for the obvious,
there is an inner aspect for understanding and
an outer aspect that obscures;
for the complete,
there is an inner aspect that hides and
an outer aspect that reveals.
Thus, to understand people is to understand oneself,
in that one can understand oneself,
but one cannot necessarily understand others.
How urgent!
Those who employ themselves, if they do not strive to be different, will be different indeed. (Or: If those who are employed don't focus on uniqueness, they will become (negatively) unique.)
There are three ways in which the *jūnzǐ* (gentleman) dislikes being different:
delighting in creating trouble,
delighting in creating the bizarre,
delighting in changing the norm.
Delighting in creating trouble leads to many complications and disturbs the masses;
delighting in creating the bizarre deviates from the Dao and confuses the common people;
delighting in changing the norm disregards laws and disrupts standards.
Therefore, reputation should not value reckless propagation,
conduct should not value reckless difficulty;
expediency is already flourishing.
Subtlety is not as good as the classics;
eloquence is considered beautiful;
but reason is not as good as its exhaustion;
refinement is considered manifest;
but the center is not as good as simplicity;
erudition is considered flourishing;
but correctness is not as good as succinctness;
none is without the Dao.
Knowing the substance of the Dao
is the ultimate greatness,
none is without the subtle.
Knowing the workings of the divine
is the ultimate subtlety,
There is nothing that does not aim to be correct.
To understand it and correct it is the height of attainment,
therefore, a *jūnzǐ* must surely maintain these three attainments.
If they are not attained,
then there is adherence but no refutation."
Someone asked about adherence.
He said:
"The sacred canon, that is all.
As for the various schools of thought,
that is called having no adherence.
There is nothing they do not put into words,
seeking its utmost attainment.
There is nothing they do not make into virtue,
making its mysteries profound.
There is nothing they do not make into the Way,
the sage makes it vast.
The Way of the sage,
is it not the Middle Way?
This is called the Nine Accesses."
Someone said:
"Achieving expression is all.
The sage, with his writings,
their innermost depths have five aspects:
They are called profound (xuán),
called subtle (miào),
called comprehensive (bāo),
called essential (yào),
About Literature.
Profound and abstruse is called xuán (玄).
Principles that are subtle are called miào (妙).
Numbers that are vast are called bāo (包).
Words that are concise are called yào (要).
Chapters that are complete are called wén (文).
The literature of the sages,
achieves these five qualities;
therefore it is said, "cannot be avoided."
The junzi (君子) delights in Heaven and understands destiny, therefore he does not worry.
He examines things carefully and distinguishes clearly, therefore he is not confused.
He settles his heart and dedicates himself to impartiality, therefore he is not afraid.
As for what he might worry and fear, there is some:
He worries that he cannot fulfill his Heaven-given nature.
He fears that he will be confused by it.
Worry cannot be avoided.
There is no confusion in Heaven's decree.
Someone asked about nature and destiny.
He replied:
"What is born is called xìng (性),
referring to form and spirit.
That which establishes life and brings it to its end is called mìng (命),
referring to good fortune and misfortune.
Indeed, in the regulations of my birth,
nature and destiny reside.
The junzi follows his nature to assist his destiny,
accepting good fortune when it comes,
If you are guarding something,
do not be insistent on your duties,
do not harbor resentment.
Those who love favor
ride on the mandate of Heaven and become arrogant;
those who love to hate
go against the mandate of Heaven and become excessive.
Therefore, arrogance leads to the failure of service,
and excess leads to the failure of preservation.
Love leads to negligence,
hate leads to extremity,
insisting on duties leads to fortune,
hating leads to misfortune,
this is delusion."
Someone asked about the mandate of Heaven and human affairs.
He said:
"There are three categories.
The upper and lower do not change,
but in between, human affairs exist.
Fate is similar,
but actions are different,
so fortune and misfortune differ.
Therefore, it is said, 'Exhaustively investigate principle and develop your nature to the point of understanding fate.'
Mèngzǐ claimed that human nature is good,
Xúnqīng claimed that human nature is evil.
Gōngsūn Zǐ said:
'Human nature is neither good nor evil.'
Yáng Xióng said:
"Human nature is a mixture of good and evil."
Liú Xiàng said:
"Nature and emotions correspond;
nature is not exclusively good,
and emotions are not exclusively evil."
Someone said:
"May I ask for the reasoning behind this?"
He said:
"If nature were good, there would be no Four Fiends;
if nature were evil, there would be no Three Worthies.
If there were no good or evil,
and King Wén's teachings were uniform,
there would be no Duke of Zhōu, Guǎn, or Cài;
if nature were good and emotions evil,
then Jié and Zhòu would have no nature, and Yáo and Shùn would have no emotions;
if nature were a mixture of both good and evil,
it would mean the highly intelligent harbor wickedness while the lowly and foolish possess goodness.
This principle
has not been fully investigated.
Only Liú Xiàng's words are reasonable."
Someone said:
"Benevolence and righteousness are part of nature,
likes and dislikes are emotions.
Benevolence and righteousness are always good, but likes and dislikes can sometimes be evil,
therefore there are evil emotions."
He said:
"Bùrán.
Likes and dislikes are the selections and rejections of human nature.
They are visibly manifested externally,
therefore they are called emotions;
they must originate from human nature.
Benevolence and righteousness are the sincerity of goodness;
why suspect that they are always good?
Likes and dislikes are where good and evil have not yet been distinguished;
why is it strange that there is evil within them?
Whenever we speak of spirit, nothing is closer to it than *qi*;
if there is *qi*, then there is form;
if there is spirit, then there are the emotions of likes, dislikes, joy, and anger.
Therefore, people have emotions
because *qi* has form;
*qi* has white and black,
spirit has good and evil.
Form and white and black go together,
emotions and good and evil go together,
therefore, black *qi* is not the fault of form,
evil emotions are not the crime of emotion."
Someone said:
"People, regarding profit,
see it and like it.
Those who can use benevolence and righteousness as a check
are those whose nature cuts off their emotions.
If nature is little and emotions are many,
and nature cannot cut off the emotions,
then emotions will act alone and become evil."
He said:
"Not so.
That is a matter of how much or little good and evil there is,
not of emotions.
If there is a person here,
To remember Zhāng Qiān 張騫 held in the Western extremities,
to think of Sū Wǔ 蘇武 at the northern borders,
and then one knows that those who cherish their family homes are truly base.
Extending this kind of thinking,
one can reach everywhere.
Let virtue be compared to those above,
let desires be compared to those below.
Virtue is compared to those above,
therefore one knows shame;
desires are compared to those below,
therefore one knows contentment.
To know shame and understand it,
then becoming a sage or worthy is within reach;
to merely know contentment,
then one's narrow-mindedness can be comfortably settled.
With sages and worthies within reach,
how could one do evil?
With narrow-mindedness comfortably settled,
how could one be extravagant?
This is called having self-restraint,
pure indeed,
that is the highest state.
The next best is simply grasping the general idea.
Nothing is outside the general idea;
grasp its general idea.
If one is without wickedness,
then that is acceptable.
The Junzi 君子 examines himself in four ways,
anger does not disorder his virtue,
and joy is not unrighteous."

1 "Governmental Structure First"
Now, the great foundation of the Way lies solely in benevolence and righteousness.i
The Five Classics are used to regulate it,
and various books are used to elaborate on it.
It is recited and sung,
played on stringed instruments and danced to.
The examples of the past are already clear,
and later generations further expound upon them.
Therefore, the ancient sage-kings,
with regard to benevolence and righteousness,
To reiterate and emphasize.
A firm order without limit,
this is called "Shen Jian" ("Cautions of Shen").
The sagely Hàn dynasty ruled all under Heaven,
respecting ancestors, they brilliantly governed the times,
their merit resonated throughout the universe.
But there were fierce ministers who disrupted the government,
and the times became desolate, ruined, and obscured.
Now, these grand guiding principles.
Taking lessons from the standards of the Three Dynasties,
the king truly pursued virtue,
and his accomplishments were esteemed.
Heaven's way is with you,
may the Emperor be greatly at rest,
ascending and descending with sincerity,
and all nations be at peace.
If one believes this,
one's actions will reach far.
Establishing the Way of Heaven,
it is said to be Yin and Yang;
establishing the Way of Earth,
it is said to be gentleness and strength;
establishing the Way of Man, it is said to be benevolence and righteousness.
Yin and Yang govern their essence and vital energy,
gentleness and strength distinguish the forms of all things,
benevolence and righteousness manage their affairs,
This is what is called the Dao.
Therefore, the grand principles of all governance
are simply law and education.
Education is the transformation of Yáng;
law is the symbol of Yīn.
Rén (仁, benevolence) is to love this;
Yì (義, righteousness) is to make this appropriate;
Lǐ (禮, ritual propriety) is to practice this;
Xìn (信, trustworthiness) is to guard this;
Zhì (智, wisdom) is to know this.
Therefore, use likes and dislikes to make them manifest;
use joy and anger to preside over them;
use sorrow and happiness to care for them.
If these two extremes are without fault,
the five virtues are not abandoned,
the six regulations are not violated,
then the three powers (Heaven, Earth, and Man) are truly ordered,
the five affairs (appearance, speech, seeing, hearing, and thinking) are all prepared,
the hundred crafts are all regulated,
and all meritorious deeds are all glorious.
Heaven makes the Dao,
the sovereign makes the ultimate standard,
the ministers act as assistants,
the people form the foundation.
Use systems to regulate them,
use achievements to record them.
The policies of the former wise kings:
first was to embrace Heaven,
second was to rectify oneself,
third was to appoint the worthy,
fourth was to care for the people,
fifth was to clarify the rules,
sixth was to establish enterprises.
Embracing Heaven should be with sincerity,
rectifying oneself should be with constancy,
appointing the worthy should be with firmness,
caring for the people should be with diligence,
clarifying the rules should be with standard,
establishing enterprises should be with sincerity,
these are called the fundamental principles of governance.
The methods for achieving good governance,
first eliminate the four evils,
then promote the five policies:
first is falsehood,
second is selfishness,
third is license,
fourth is extravagance.
Falsehood disrupts customs,
selfishness corrupts laws,
license transgresses norms,
extravagance destroys systems.
If these four are not removed,
then governance cannot be carried out.
When customs are chaotic, the Way is neglected;
even Heaven and Earth cannot preserve their nature.
When laws are broken, the world is overturned;
even rulers cannot maintain their standards.
When rules are transgressed, ritual is lost;
even sages cannot fully realize their Way.
When regulations fail, desires run rampant;
even the four corners of the earth cannot satisfy their demands.
These are called the four calamities.
Promote agriculture and sericulture to nourish their lives;
discern likes and dislikes to rectify their customs;
propagate education to illuminate their transformation;
establish military preparedness to uphold their authority;
make clear rewards and punishments to govern their laws.
These are called the five policies.
If the people do not fear death,
they cannot be deterred by punishments;
if the people do not enjoy life,
they cannot be encouraged by good deeds.
Even if Xiè were to spread the five teachings,
and Gāo Yáo were to serve as the minister of justice,
governance would not succeed.
Therefore, those in authority should first enrich the people's wealth to secure their ambition.
The emperor should cultivate the sacred field,
and the empress should cultivate silkworms in the palace.
There should be no idle people in the country,
and no uncultivated fields in the countryside.
Do not waste wealth,
do not exert strength carelessly.
Use them to attend to the people's affairs.
This is called nurturing life.
That which the *jūnzǐ* uses to move Heaven and Earth,
respond to the spirits,
rectify the myriad things, and achieve kingly rule,
must be rooted in truth and reality.
Therefore, those in positions of authority should carefully examine the standards and principles by which to determine likes and dislikes.
Good and evil should be judged based on merit and demerit.
Praise and blame should be based on reliable evidence.
Listen to words and hold responsible for actions.
Promote reputations and examine the reality [behind them].
Allow no fraud, deceit, excess, or trickery to unsettle the hearts of the people.
Therefore, no affair should be left uninvestigated,
no matter left unaddressed,
no goodness left unrevealed,
no evil left unexposed,
no customs with deceit and strangeness,
no people with excessive and disordered behavior.
When the common people, both high and low, see that benefit and harm depend on themselves,
then they will respectfully and sincerely compose their minds,
carefully cultivate their conduct,
have no internal delusions or confusions,
and have no external improper desires.
Let them consider what they may be deprived of.
Those with crimes and wickedness will have no hope of good fortune,
Those without offense or fault do not worry or fear.
Entreaties and requests are not heeded.
Wealth and bribes are of no use.
Then the people's minds are at peace.
This is called straightening customs.
The jūnzǐ (君子) are influenced by emotions.
The xiǎorén (小人) are influenced by punishments.
Honor and shame are the essence of rewards and punishments.
Therefore, ritual teachings and honor/shame,
are applied to the jūnzǐ (君子),
to transform their emotions;
shackles and floggings
are applied to the xiǎorén (小人),
to govern their legal punishments.
The jūnzǐ (君子) do not commit acts worthy of shame,
much less acts worthy of legal punishment!
The xiǎorén (小人) do not fear legal punishment,
much less shame!
As for those of the middle class,
both punishments and rituals are applied to them.
When teachings and transformations are abandoned,
people of the middle class are pushed and fall into the realm of the xiǎorén (小人).
When teachings and transformations are practiced,
people of the middle class are led and brought onto the path of the jūnzǐ (君子).
This is called clarifying transformation.
The disposition of the xiǎorén (小人) is such that,
If relaxation is allowed, then pride arises;
if pride arises, then indulgence results;
if indulgence results, then haste ensues;
if haste ensues, then resentment follows;
if resentment follows, then rebellion occurs;
in peril, they plot disorder.
In peace, they ponder desires;
without might and strength, there is no way to restrain them.
Therefore, those in positions of authority
must have military preparedness
to guard against the unforeseen,
and to suppress predatory violence.
In peaceful times, this is entrusted to internal administration;
in times of trouble, it is employed in the military.
This is called wielding authority.
Rewards and punishments are the handle of governance.
Clearly reward and certainly punish,
carefully consider trust and be cautious in issuing orders,
reward to encourage good,
punish to deter evil.
The ruler does not reward indiscriminately,
not merely because he cherishes his wealth;
if rewards are given indiscriminately, then good will not be encouraged.
He does not punish indiscriminately,
not merely because he is cautious in using punishment.
If punishments are inflicted indiscriminately, then evil will not be deterred.
If rewards do not encourage, it is called stopping goodness;
To punish but not effectively is called condoning evil.
If those in authority can but prevent their subordinates from doing good,
and not condone their doing evil,
then the state will be well-governed.
This is called unified law.
Once the four calamities are removed,
and the five administrative measures are established,
implement them with sincerity,
and uphold them with firmness;
be simple but not negligent,
be relaxed but not remiss;
achieve through inaction,
let things implement themselves;
manage through non-interference,
let things interact on their own.
Achieve completion without severity,
govern without harshness,
and by simply folding one's hands and yielding in ceremony, the whole world will be at peace.
This is called the way of governance.
It is essential to cultivate the six principles to establish the standard of the Way:
First is Centrality (Zhōng),
Second is Harmony (Hé),
Third is Rectitude (Zhèng),
Fourth is Impartiality (Gōng),
Fifth is Sincerity (Chéng),
Sixth is Adaptability (Tōng);
Using the way of Heaven as the standard of balance,
using the way of Earth as the standard of harmony,
using benevolence and virtue as the standard of uprightness,
using matters and affairs as the standard of impartiality,
using self-cultivation to the utmost as the standard of sincerity,
using variability as the standard of open communication;
this is called the reality of the Dao.
Be concerned with ten difficulties in employing the worthy and capable:
first is not knowing them,
second is not promoting them,
third is not entrusting them (with responsibility),
fourth is not seeing them through (to the end),
fifth is discarding great virtue for small grudges,
sixth is dismissing great merit for small faults,
seventh is concealing great beauty with small flaws,
eighth is harming loyalty and integrity with treacherous slander,
ninth is disrupting proper standards with heretical doctrines,
tenth is abolishing the worthy and capable through slander and jealousy.
These are called the ten difficulties.
If the ten difficulties are not eliminated,
then worthy ministers will not be employed;
if worthy ministers are not employed,
then the state is not truly a state.
Observe the nine prevailing tendencies to determine the constant state of the country:
first is order,
second is decline,
The third is weakness,
the fourth is discord,
the fifth is chaos,
the sixth is desolation,
the seventh is rebellion,
the eighth is peril,
the ninth is ruin.
When ruler and minister are close and observe propriety;
when the officials are harmonious yet diverse,
yielding and not contending,
diligent and not resentful;
when in times of peace, each one performs their duty,
this is the way of a well-governed state.
When customs are not uniform,
positions are not respected,
petty officials slander and are jealous,
commoners make pronouncements,
this is the way of a declining state.
When the ruler loves yielding,
the ministers love ease,
the scholars love to travel,
the people love to wander,
this is the way of a weak state.
When ruler and minister contend for fame,
the court contends for merit,
scholar-officials contend for reputation,
commoners contend for profit,
this is the way of a state in discord.
The ruler has too many desires;
the subordinates engage in too many tricks;
the laws are not fixed;
the government has too many factions—
these are the characteristics of a chaotic state.
To consider extravagance as breadth,
to consider arrogance as loftiness,
to consider excess as understanding,
to call adherence to rituals "strenuous,"
to call upholding the law "rigid"—
these are the characteristics of a dissolute state.
To consider harshness as meticulousness,
to consider personal gain as public interest,
to consider exploiting subordinates as capability,
to consider pandering to superiors as loyalty—
these are the characteristics of a rebellious state.
Superiors and subordinates are distant from each other;
those inside and outside deceive each other;
petty officials vie for favor;
high officials vie for power—
these are the characteristics of a state in peril.
The ruler does not inquire of the lower levels;
the lower levels do not remonstrate with the ruler;
the words of women are heeded;
private affairs are conducted as government;
these are the characteristics of a state facing destruction.
Therefore, the ruler must carefully observe the state's customs.
Be cautious in all legal cases, so as to illuminate human feelings.
The greatest virtue of Heaven and Earth is life;
The greatest extreme for all things is death.
The dead cannot be brought back to life,
The punished cannot be restored.
Therefore, in the punishments of the former kings,
officials and teachers were used to carry them out,
thorns and Chinese locust trees were used to make judgments,
truthful interrogation was used to grant leniency,
the court and marketplace were used to share the responsibility,
pity and compassion were used to provide relief.
Once punishment is decided,
joyous music is not performed,
this is the utmost caution.
Punishment, oh, punishment,
how careful it must be!
Carefully examine the five pardons, so as to pacify the people in moderation:
The first is to examine the original intention (of the crime),
the second is to manifest virtue,
the third is to encourage meritorious service,
the fourth is to praise transformation (through moral influence),
the fifth is to consider expedient measures.
All that the former kings pardoned
must belong to these categories,
if not belonging to these categories,
such crimes must never be pardoned.
Tiānzǐ yǒu sìshí:
In the morning, he listens to matters of state;
During the day, he makes inquiries;
In the evening, he revises and issues decrees;
At night, he rests.
Above him are teachers and tutors;
Below him are banqueting ministers;
On a grand scale, there are lectures on learning;
On a small scale, there is consultation.
He does not reject straightforward speech;
He is not ashamed to ask those below him;
Public and private affairs are without fault;
Outer and inner affairs are not different;
This is called having good relationships.
He who asks clearly about governance will have a close-knit rule.
"The root of all things lies in the person;
The root of the realm lies in the family;
The root of order and chaos lies in those on the left and right;
When inner correctness is established, the four cardinal directions are settled."
He who asks thoroughly about the Way will maintain simplicity.
"There is one word that can be constantly practiced: *forgiveness* (*shù*);
There is one action that can be constantly followed: *uprightness* (*zhèng*).
Forgiveness is the method of benevolence;
Uprightness is the essence of righteousness.
How perfect!
This is called the root of the Way;
All transformations reside therein.
This is called obtaining without thinking,
and accomplishing without acting.
Hold it within your breast and heart,
and its efficacy will cover all under Heaven.”
From the Son of Heaven down to the common people,
likes and dislikes, sorrow and joy,
their cultivation should be the same.
Abundance and scarcity, labor and ease,
each has its proper measure.
Above, it is sufficient to fulfill ritual;
below, it is sufficient to fulfill music.
This is what is called the Great Way.
All under Heaven and the state are a single body.
The ruler is the head,
the ministers are the arms,
and the people are the hands and feet.
If those below suffer hardship,
then those above cannot fully enjoy pleasure.
If those below are hungry,
then those above cannot have complete meals.
If those below are cold,
then those above cannot have complete clothing.
To be barefoot while wearing ceremonial tassels
is not proper.
Therefore, cold feet injure the heart;
a cold populace injures the state.
Asking a sovereign about the ultimate way (dào) to guide the people:
the people use the ultimate beautiful things to nourish the sovereign.
The sovereign bestows his benevolence,
the people elevate their labor.
This is a reciprocal relationship that goes everywhere,
the meaning of mutual return.
Therefore, the abundance of things in a time of great peace
is not extreme desire;
the loss of things and the deficiency of ritual
is not humility and frugality.
The principle is thus.
Asking whether the ruler of the people should have public levies and no private demands,
public expenses and no private waste,
public service and no private employ,
public rewards and no private favors,
public anger and no private grudges.
Private demands lead to subordinates being vexed and without limit;
this is called harming purity.
Private waste leads to officials being depleted and without end;
this is called harming regulation.
Private employ leads to the people being disturbed and without measure;
this is called harming righteousness.
Private favors lead to subordinates having empty hopes and without standard;
this is called harming uprightness.
Private grudges lead to subordinates being suspicious and insecure;
this is called harming virtue.
Asking about those who are good at governing the people,
it is governing their nature.
Someone said:
"Smelting metal causes it to flow;
if the fire is removed, it becomes hard.
Agitating water makes it rise;
if left alone, it will fall.
How can it be governed?"
I say:
"If the fire is not removed, it will always flow;
if agitated without ceasing, it will always rise.
Therefore, the furnace of a great smelter
can prevent it from ever becoming hard.
The device for raising water
can prevent it from ever falling.
One who is good at establishing teachings is like this,
then it will be governed for life.
Therefore, any vessel can be made to share the same direction as Yán Rǎn,
if a hundred gold pieces are placed before it,
and a white blade is added to its body,
even the great Zhí would not dare to pick it up.
One who is good at establishing laws is like this,
then he will not pick it up for life.
Therefore, Zhí can be made to share the same merit as Bó Yí."
Asking whether the people are like water.
"Those who cross great rivers, the best take boats,
the next best swim.
A swimmer exerts effort and faces danger;
one who rides a boat is relaxed and safe.
Entering the water empty-handed will surely lead to drowning.
To govern the people with knowledge and ability is like swimming;
to govern the people with morality is like a boat.
Indulging the people's desires is called chaos;
suppressing the people's desires is called desolation."
He said:
"Then what should be done?"
He said:
"Set boundaries for them,
so that they do not overstep them.
Set limits for their land, so that they do not overstep them either.
Thus, water can be prevented from overflowing,
but it cannot be prevented from flowing.
One who is good at forbidding
first forbids himself and then others;
one who is not good at forbidding
first forbids others and then himself.
The best forbidding leads to no forbidding at all,
and commands are the same.
If one indulges his own desires and uses the law to restrain the desires of the people,
practices deception in officialdom and demands honesty from the people,
seeks to acquire what he already has in excess,
and takes away what the people lack,
abandons what is easy for himself,
and demands what is difficult from others,
this is the root of resentment.
Saying the source of principle is thus severed.
For those above governing those below,
it is like a fisherman,
concealing (the line) in the hand,
responding at the hook,
then one can catch fish.
For those near governing those far,
it is like controlling a horse,
harmonizing with the hand and adjusting at the bit,
then one can make the horse obey.
Therefore, the essence of the supreme Dao
is not in the person, (but) the Dao.
Observing a child driving chickens, one can see the method of governing the people:
a child driving chickens,
if (the driving) is too hurried, (the chickens) are startled;
if (the driving) is too slow, (the chickens) are sluggish.
When (the chickens) are heading north,
suddenly intercept them,
then they will turn and cross to the south;
when (the chickens) are heading south,
suddenly intercept them,
then they will turn and cross to the north.
If pressed too hard, they will fly;
if too loosely managed, they will run free.
If (their) will is idle, (one should) associate with them;
if (their) flow is slow and they are uneasy, then feed them.
To drive without driving
is the ultimate in driving.
If the will is settled and secure, then one follows the proper path and enters the gate.
The highest (ruler) does not empty the markets,

sacrifices and jade and silk are used to make the prayers and beseechings clear;
auspicious new moons are used to communicate with them.
'The *Lǐ* says, the *Lǐ* says:
Does it merely refer to jade and silk?'
To 'please' and to 'beseech',
does it merely refer to wine and food?
If it is not the proper *Lǐ*, then perhaps there will be transgressions;
if it is not the proper request, then there will be no response."
Someone asked:
"Is praying and beseeching permissible?"
He said:
"If it is a matter of *qì* and things responding to stimuli, then it is permissible;
if it is a matter of inherent nature and destiny, then it is not."
Someone asked:
"Is it possible to avoid illness and misfortune?"
Is there such a thing?"
He said:
"Illness and misfortune, what are they?
They affect either the body or the spirit;
the body cannot be avoided,
the spirit cannot be escaped.
What can be avoided is not the body,
what can be escaped is not the spirit.
Maintain oneself by following Heaven,
and even for ten thousand *lǐ*, one will not err.
It is like a child covering his eyes and hiding in the armpit of a giant, saying he is escaping.
Is that possible?"
Someone asked:
"Human forms possess *xiàng* (appearances)."
The reply was:
"Indeed, that is so.
The mutual embracing of *shénqì* (spirit and vital energy) and *xíngróng* (appearance)
is natural.
To add to it with conduct,
and to consider it in light of the times,
they complement each other,
and also partially undermine each other.
The variations are many,
the transformations are numerous.
There are also superior, middle, and inferior grades, that is all."
Someone asked about the arts of spiritual immortals.
The reply was:
"How absurd!
It is a trivial pursuit!
Sages do not study it,
not because they dislike life,
but because beginning and end are destiny,
and shortness and length are fate.
Destiny is not something that human effort can accomplish."
Someone asked:
"Are there also immortals?"
He replied:
"The Jiāoyáo and Guìmǎng tribes,
born in strange lands,
if they have immortals,
are also of a different kind."
Someone asked:
"Are there people who live for hundreds of years?"
He replied:
"For strength we mention Wū Huò,
for swiftness we speak of Qiāng Hài,
for courage we look to Bēn and Yù,
for sagehood we speak of Zhòng Ní,
for longevity we mention Péng Zǔ.
Things have their outstanding individuals,
this cannot be denied."
Someone asked:
"Those who are long-lived must have the Dào;
it is not due to the effort of practice."
He replied:
"Indeed, only with longevity
can one truly utilize the Dào.
Only by utilizing the Dào
can one's nature be long-lived.
If it is not in one's nature,
Cultivation does not arrive.
Learning must lead to sagehood,
in order to fully realize one's nature;
longevity must employ the Dao,
in order to fully realize one's destiny."
Someone asked:
"Are there people who transform themselves and become immortals?
Is this believable?"
The answer:
"I have never heard of it before.
In that case, it is a transformation, not immortality.
There are cases of men turning into women,
and cases of the dead coming back to life.
But how can this be human nature?
The natural order is not preserved in these."
Someone asked:
"Is there a way to nurture one's nature?"
The answer:
"To nurture one's nature, hold onto the center and harmony,
and guard it for the sake of life.
To love relatives, love virtue, love strength, and love the spirits is called frugality;
otherwise, it is not proper to express them;
excess leads to lack of ease.
Therefore, a gentleman regulates the expression of his Qi,
not allowing it to become blocked, stagnated, or bottomed out.
Confused and chaotic actions lead to illness,
Therefore, joy, anger, sorrow, happiness, thought, and worry must each attain their proper place;
this is how to nourish the spirit.
Cold, warmth, emptiness, fullness, growth, and decline must each attain their proper place;
this is how to nourish the body.
One who is good at governing qi
is like Yǔ governing the waters.
As for guiding and leading qi, accumulating qi,
traversing the viscera, and internal visualization,
excess leads to losing the center.
These can treat illness,
but are not the sacred arts of nourishing nature.
Bending comes from extending,
accumulating comes from emptying,
inwardness comes from outwardness;
qi should be dispersed, yet it is suppressed;
the body should be harmonized, yet it is corrected;
the spirit should be balanced, yet it is restrained;
inevitably there will be disharmony.
One who is good at nourishing nature has no fixed methods;
attaining harmony is enough.
Two inches from the navel is called the *guān* (gate);
the *guān* is what encloses and stores the breath of qi,
in order to impart it to the four limbs.
Therefore, one whose qi is long breathes with the *guān*;
one whose qi is short, their breath rises slightly,
their pulse becomes slightly hurried,
their spirit becomes slightly scattered.
As for breathing with the shoulders and the qi expanding,
If one's spirit is slightly focused,
to the point where one's breath emanates from the *guān* (關, vital point), then one's *qi* will spread forth.
Therefore, those who cultivate the Dao constantly direct their *qi* to the *guān*,
this is called an essential skill.
Generally, *yang qi* generates and nourishes,
*yin qi* diminishes and kills.
Those who are harmonious and cheerful,
their *qi* is *yang*.
Therefore, those who cultivate their nature,
should elevate their *yang* and suppress their *yin*.
When *yang* reaches its extreme, it leads to excess;
when *yin* reaches its extreme, it leads to stagnation.
Excess leads to regret,
stagnation leads to misfortune.
Now, things cannot create spring,
so they await the spring of Heaven to be born.
But humans are not like that,
we simply preserve our own spring.
Medicine, that is, treatment,
is that which is used to cure disease.
If there is no disease,
then there is no need for medicine.
Meat cannot overcome (i.e. is inferior to) the *qi* of food,
how much less so medicine?
Cold induces heat,
heat then causes stagnation.
This is the effect of *yin* medicine,
only when appropriate does it not cause harm.
If one's *qi* is balanced,
then there must be injury.
It is just the same with acupuncture and fire.
Therefore, those who nourish their nature do not take too much [medicine];
it is only a matter of moderation."
Someone asked:
"The benevolent live long,
what does this mean?"
He said:
"The benevolent do not harm their nature internally,
nor do they harm things externally;
they do not go against Heaven above,
nor do they go against people below.
They dwell in righteousness and reside in the center,
their form and spirit are in harmony,
therefore misfortune does not arrive and good fortune gathers,
this is the method of longevity."
He said:
"What about Yán Rǎn?"
He said:
"It is fate.
Wheat does not last through summer,
flowers do not survive spring,
how can harmonious *qi* [be maintained]?
Although it is said that they are short-lived,
longevity is also within them."
Or someone asked about the sort of people who practice alchemy (
He said:
"Fù Yì's discussion of it is appropriate.
To fire clay to make tiles is possible,
but to melt tiles to make bronze is impossible.
To verify the impossible with the natural,
is strange indeed.
To use dog and sheep meat to create horses and cattle,
is nearly the same,
isn't it likely so?
The world claims the apocryphal texts (wěishū)
are the work of Zhòng Ní.
Chén Yuè's uncle, the former Minister of Public Works Shuǎng, refuted them,
and revealed their falseness.
Could they have originated before the revival period of the Hòu Hàn dynasty,
and be the work of followers of Zhāng?"
Someone asked:
"Does it mix oneself with Zhòng Ní,
or mix Zhòng Ní with oneself?
As for those, they only mix Zhòng Ní with themselves.
In that case, one can say that the eighty-one sections
are not the work of Zhòng Ní."
Someone asked:
"Should they be burned?"
He said:
"If they are not the work of Zhòng Ní, then no,
but if there is something to be taken from them, then it's acceptable.
Why burn them?
The one in a superior position does not accept empty words,
does not listen to frivolous schemes,
does not adopt flowery reputations,
does not promote false affairs.
Words must have a purpose,
schemes must have a basis in classics;
reputation must have substance,
affairs must have accomplishment."

Someone asked:
"Why should a *jūnzǐ* (gentleman) devote himself to learning?"
The answer is:
"Those who are born with knowledge are few;
those who acquire knowledge through learning are many.
The vast majority of people,
the careless scholars,
clear governance,
chaotic disorder—
all are due to the rise and fall of learning.
Is it not fitting to devote oneself to it?"
A *jūnzǐ* has three mirrors:
the world as a mirror,
the past as a lesson,
people as wise,
and a mirror as clear.
The decline of the Xià and Shāng dynasties
did not take warning from Yǔ and Tāng.
The problems of the Zhōu and Qín dynasties
did not take warning from the common people.
A slanted cap and a dirty face
do not take warning from a clear mirror.
Therefore, the wise person only concerns himself with taking warning;
as for glancing at the reflection, that's like having no mirror at all.
Someone asked:
"The key to achieving order,
is it the ruler?"
I replied:
"It requires both to stand together.
Just as heaven and earth do not produce things alone,
so ruler and ministers do not achieve order alone.
That which initiates things is heaven and earth;
that which governs them is ruler and ministers!
The way of the former kings placed great emphasis on instruction;
therefore, there wasn't even a moment when they deviated from the Way.
In the past, there were those who highly esteemed sagacity,
proceeding by teaching and admonishing,
relying on assistance and guidance,
and respectfully harmonizing with the four neighboring states.
Therefore, officials who controlled the caged beasts
were never absent from their side;
the standards of propriety and law
were never out of sight;
The words of the wise men of the past,
do not cease to be practiced;
unrighteous paths,
do not proclaim in your heart;
then perverse qi,
will have no way to enter.
If there is a gap,
there will certainly be those who enter.
Therefore, when perverse ambitions arise, perverse actions follow,
when perverse actions follow, righteousness is blocked,
when righteousness is blocked, then fairness also has no way to enter.
Not employing those one loves is called impartiality;
only following what is impartial is called enlightenment.
Duke Huán of Qí, was of average talent,
and yet he was able to achieve great undertakings,
because he had something different.
Concubines filled his palace,
and it wasn't that he didn't have favorites;
officials filled his court,
and it wasn't that he didn't have those to whom he was close.
But outwardly, he entrusted Guǎn Zhòng, who had shot at him,
and Wèi Jī, despite her being a concubine of beautiful appearance,
not because he loved them,
but because he entrusted them.
Only then did he know that the unworthy cannot be entrusted,
and the unwise cannot be followed.
Oh, how magnificent was this undertaking!
When the region between the heart and diaphragm is pure white,
If the Èr Shù 二豎 do not arise,
this is called the heart being at peace.
If the inner palace is pure and tranquil,
and favored concubines and illegitimate offspring do not arise,
this is called the government being at peace.
Now, the gāo huāng 膏肓 is close to the heart and in a dangerous place,
needles cannot reach it,
medicine cannot hit it,
and attacking it is impossible.
The Èr Shù 二豎 hide there,
this is called a serious illness.
Therefore, those who govern themselves and govern the state
should only fear this."
Someone asked:
"Is loving the people like one's children
the ultimate in benevolence?"
He said:
"Not yet."
He asked:
"Is loving the people like one's own body
the ultimate in benevolence?"
He said:
"Not yet.
Tāng 湯 prayed in the Sanglín 桑林,
Zhū 邾 moved to Yì 繹,
Jǐng 景 sacrificed to avert drought.
This can be called loving the people."
He said:
"Why value the people and devalue oneself?"
He said:
"The ruler receives the mandate of Heaven in order to nourish the people.
If the people exist, then the state exists;
if the people perish, then the state perishes.
Therefore, valuing the people
is valuing the state and receiving the mandate of Heaven."
Someone asked:
"Mèng Kē (孟軻) said that everyone can become Yáo (堯) or Shùn (舜).
Is that really true?"
He said:
"If a person is not of the lowest intelligence,
then he can become Yáo (堯) or Shùn (舜).
To resemble Yáo (堯) or Shùn (舜) in appearance
or to have the same surname as Yáo (堯) or Shùn (舜)
is not necessary.
To wear the clothes of Yáo (堯),
and practice the Way of Yáo (堯),
then it is possible.
Practiced in the past,
one is the Yáo (堯) or Shùn (舜) of antiquity;
practiced in the future,
one is the Yáo (堯) or Shùn (舜) of the present."
Someone asked:
"Can everyone become Jié (桀) or Zhòu (紂)?"
He said:
「Xíng Jié, Zhòu zhī shì,
shì Jié Zhòu yě.
The deeds of Yáo, Shùn, Jié, and Zhòu
constantly coexist in the world;
it is only a matter of what people make use of.
Yáng Zhū wept at the crossroads;
what he lamented was the pressure of the many paths.
But why should the crossroads be so tragic?
Return to the center!
As for the threshold of a hanging weight,
it is simply a matter of lifting your foot.
The signs of loss and gain
are subtle, yet manifest.
When Zhào acquired two cities,
he worried when faced with tribute.
When Táo Zhū became rich,
his concubines wailed in sorrow.
This demonstrates understanding that gain can turn into loss, and loss into gain.
The patterns of bending and stretching
are hidden, yet apparent.
The distress of Yǒu Rēng
was the seed of the restoration of Xià.
The strange appearance of the pheasant in the cauldron
was a portent of the rise of Yīn.
The troubles of Shào Gōng
were a response to the flourishing of Zhōu.
The refuge at Kuài Jī
was the foundation for the hegemony of Yuè.
The turmoil of Zǐ Zhī
was a sign of a strong Yān.
This knows that extending oneself by bending oneself is the way to extend oneself."
The worry of a ruler
constantly lies between two difficulties.
Being in a position of authority and the state not being well-governed
is a difficulty.
Governing the state
then requires diligent effort, painful thought, and suppressing one's emotions to follow the Dao;
this is a difficulty.
The difficult difficulty
is what a benighted ruler chooses.
The difficulty of no difficulty
is what an enlightened ruler dwells in.
The worry of a minister
constantly lies between two crimes.
Being in office and not fully pursuing the path of loyalty and directness
is a crime.
Fully pursuing the path of loyalty and directness
inevitably means contradicting superiors and offending inferiors;
this is a crime.
The crime of having committed a crime
is what a wicked minister engages in.
The crime of having committed no crime
is what a loyal minister is placed in.
The duty of a minister
is not to say, "My lord is capable,
"He does not need me,
my words are of no help."
And yet, he does not exhaust his loyalty;
does not say, "My lord is incapable,
he does not recognize me,
my words are of no benefit."
And yet, he does not exhaust his loyalty.
One must exhaust his sincerity,
clarify his principles,
fulfill his duty,
and then let it be.
If that is not enough,
then respectfully retire,
that is the way of a minister.
Therefore, the relationship between ruler and minister should have differences but no discord,
have resentment but no regret,
have yielding but no humiliation.
A minister has three sins:
first is leading astray,
second is flattering errors,
third is holding onto favor without merit;
using wrong to lead the ruler is called leading astray,
following the ruler's wrongs is called flattering,
seeing wrong and not speaking out is called holding onto favor without merit;
the minister who leads astray is executed,
the minister who flatters is punished,
the minister who holds onto favor without merit is dismissed.
There are three ways to advance loyalty:
One is prevention (fáng),
two is rescue (jiù),
three is admonishment (jiè);
addressing something before it happens is called prevention;
stopping it after it has occurred is called rescue;
holding one accountable after the action is done is called admonishment;
Prevention is the best,
rescue is second best,
admonishment is the worst.
If those below are not silenced,
and those above do not block their ears,
then there is a chance of hearing [the truth].
A gag that can be seen
can still be removed;
a gag that is unseen
is difficult indeed.
A blockage that can be seen
can still be removed;
a blockage that is unseen
is very serious indeed.
Someone asked:
"Is there compromise for those in positions of power?"
I say:
"Those in positions of power extend themselves through righteousness,
and compromise through righteousness.
Although Gāozǔ 高祖 was able to exert his power over Qín 秦 and Xiàng 項,
he compromised before the Four Elders of Mount Shāng 商山四公;
Guāngwǔ 光武 was able to assert himself against Wǎng 莽,
but yielded to the unyielding magistrate.
Míngdì 明帝 was able to enforce his decrees throughout the realm,
but yielded to the Director of the Secretariat, Zhōnglí 鍾離.
If the Second Emperor of Qín 秦 asserted his desires while scoffing at Táng 唐 and Yú 虞,
if the Empress Dowager of Dìngtáo 定陶, Fù 傅, asserted her intentions and held a grudge against Zhèng 鄭,
this is what is meant by "not yielding."
If it were not so,
then the Zhào 趙 clan would not have been destroyed,
and Qín 秦 would have no faults.
Therefore, a ruler asserts himself based on righteousness
and yields based on righteousness.
Joy should be like the spring sun,
anger like the autumn frost,
authority like the thunder's shock,
and grace like the descent of rain and dew.
In such abundance, who can resist it?"
Someone said it would be difficult to implement.
The speaker replied:
"If Gāozǔ 高祖 had listened to the soldiers on garrison duty not wanting to be at home,
or moved the Emperor's chariot without waiting for a full day;
if Emperor Xiàowén 孝文 did not cherish thousand-li horses,
or if Lady Shèn 慎's clothes dragged on the ground;
or if Guāngwǔ 光武 did not hold pearls and jade in his hand,
it could be said that things are difficult.
If one does not restrain their emotions and cut off desires,
and is not like this,
Few are those who can succeed.
Ministers like Jīn Rìdī,
who killed his son for his private disrespect;
Bǐng Jí who didn't boast of his merits;
Sū Wǔ who firmly maintained his integrity;
they can be said to be rare."
Someone asked about cultivating ambition.
He said:
"Like Yīn Gāozōng who was able to cultivate his virtue,
using bitter medicine to cure disease;
Wèi Wǔ offering warnings and admonitions at court;
Gōujiàn hanging a gall bladder by his seat;
how vigorous!"
"To dote on one's wife and love one's concubines
is fortunate;
but the disaster it causes
is profound.
Disaster and fortune,
are they the same?"
He said:
"If you succeed, it is a celebration;
if you fail, it is a disaster.
Lady Qī's misfortune was not being made into a human pig;
Zhào Zhāoyí's misfortune was not losing her life;
Lì Jī's misfortune was not being deposed;
Gōuyì's misfortune was not dying young with her son;
if not disaster, what else?
If it were the wisdom of Lady Shèn,
the virtue of Bān Jiéyú,
the virtue of Empress Míngdé,
it would be excellent."
Those who worry and rejoice for the world
are the aspirations of a gentleman;
those who do not worry and rejoice for the world
are the aspirations of a petty person.
In an era of great peace,
affairs are leisurely and the people universally rejoice.
To have someone in a hurry perform ceremonial bows repeatedly
is not proper;
to have someone in mourning play stringed instruments and drums
is not joyous.
Ritual is simply about reverence,
music is simply about harmony.
Even commoners, both men and women, living in the fields
must have ritual and music present.
To disobey the ruler but accord with the Way
is called a loyal minister;
to disobey the Way but accord with the ruler
is called a flattering minister.
Loyalty is what benefits the ruler,
flattery is what benefits oneself.
A loyal minister finds peace in his heart,
a flattering minister finds peace in his body.
Therefore, those in positions of authority must observe what is contrary and what is compliant,
be discerning about what they do,
and be cautious about where they settle.
The King of Guǎngchuān (廣川王) did not observe,
therefore he killed his ministers.
King Gōng of Chǔ (楚恭王) observed it but was too late,
therefore there were dying words.
King Xuān of Qí (齊宣王) certainly observed it,
therefore he rewarded those who remonstrated.
Someone asked about the warnings for rulers and ministers.
I said,
"Nothing is not a warning."
"May I ask for the essentials?"
I said,
"A ruler should be warned against exclusive desires,
and a minister should be warned against exclusive profits."

fú néng kè, but they could not overcome them,
gù Táng, Xià píng. therefore the Táng and Xià dynasties were stable.
Nán Zhī Wēi gōng Wén Gōng, Nán Zhī Wēi attacked Wén Gōng,

bù néng kè, but they could not overcome them,

yī yán zhī kòu xí yú xīxià, the attack of a single word whispered beneath the knees,

fùxīn zhī rén, loyal and sincere persons,

Gù míngwáng shèn nèishǒu, Therefore, enlightened rulers are careful of internal defense,

Clouds follow the dragon,
wind follows the tiger,
the phoenix appears during the Sháo music,
the qilin gathers at the location of Kǒng (Confucius);
this is correspondence.
It originates from this,
and corresponds to that;
goodness results in auspiciousness,
auspiciousness results in blessings;
otherwise, there is misfortune,
misfortune results in blame;
therefore, the junzi responds accordingly."
The junzi eats harmonious soup to balance his qi,
listens to harmonious sounds to balance his will.
Accepts harmonious words to balance his governance,
conducts harmonious actions to balance his virtue.
Now, sour and salty, sweet and bitter are different,
but good flavors are combined to make what is called harmonious soup.
The notes Gong, Shang, Jiao, and Zheng are different,
but good sounds are expressed,
this is called harmonious sound.
Praise and criticism, gain and loss are different,
but using centeredness and correctness to teach,
this is called harmonious words.
Going forth and staying back, movement and stillness are different,
but using elegant measures to balance,
this is called harmonious actions.
Someone said:
"If one's words are such that no one dares to disagree,
then that is close to losing the state."
Kǒngzǐ said:
"The gentleman harmonizes but does not conform."
Yàn Zǐ also said:
"If one dilutes water with water,
who can eat it?
If the qín and sè play only one note,
who can listen to it?"
The *Shī* (Book of Poetry) says:
"There is also harmonious soup,
already flavored and balanced.
In offering sacrifice there is no speaking,
at times there is no contention."
This is what is meant.

Yet not to cherish its brightness,

If one's proper role is settled, then one will not be excessive.
It is said:
"Talent is the substance;
conduct is what can be done;
talent is what cannot be done."
It is said:
"What the ancients called talent was fundamental;
what people today call talent is superficial.
Therefore, regarding the value of conduct,
one should not lose their talent, but talent can be lost.
The ancients had a saying:
'One who goes towards Chǔ but drives the chariot north.'
He says:
'My horses are good,
my expenses are high,
my driver is skilled.'
The more these three increase,
the further he is from Chǔ.
Follow the road and gallop,
respond to the directions and move,
the *jūnzǐ* has conduct,
and conduct will surely arrive."
